# Data Processing: Generate Variables {#sec-walker-make-variables}



At the end of @sec-walker-data-importing we had four dataframes: `df.adm` (applications), `df.hd` (directory information), `df.rank` (rankings), and `df.policy` (state policy).

Ultimately, we want *one* dataframe, with one row per school per year, that has:

- the policy variable we wish to study

- the outcome variable that we'll use to measure the policy impact

- and variables that will be used to show how the outcomes might differ by group – heterogeneous impacts.

This chapter just builds the variables, in that order. Like before, the goal is to generate a readbale and workflow.

## Recall the Dataframes

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Coding Learning Objectives"}
- `source()`
:::

Empirical projects can get overwhelming. There is simply *so much* to do. One way to help with that is to focus on small tasks and write self-contained scripts. Think of this as chapters in your book. Each chapter advances the story in a way that is well-described by the chapter title. At the end of @sec-walker-data-importing, we saved *import data.R* in `scripts/data processing`. That script generated four dataframes (it might be good to go back and add a comment at the top of the script as to what it does so future you doesn't have to read the whole thing to figure out!).

Now, we need those four dataframes in our *Environment* (upper right of Rstudio) in order to combine them. Let's assume you've taken a (well-deserved) break after generating *import data.R*, closed down R, and have just re-opened it. You can get the dataframes back into your *Environment* by opening *import data.R* and running the script with Code –\> Run Region –\> Run All. Intuitively, you are going to the script that is the origin, or source, of the dataframes. Fortunately, R provides a way to automate that -- `source()` -- which takes a file path as an argument and executes the file verbatim.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: `source()`"}
Keep scripts as separate files whose name (or path) indicates what they do. Call the scripts with `source()`.
:::

Run it in the console and the four dataframes are back:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source(here("scripts","data processing","import data.R")) #or whatever you named your script
```
:::


Our new script will *assume* that has been done, and say so in a comment on its first line. Recording your assumptions right where the next reader will trip over them is cheap insurance – and at the end of the unit, one master script will make sure everything actually runs in the right order.

## Policy Variable

Generally, we want to study the impact of a policy on some outcome. In this context, the impact of *bans* on the *share of women applicants*.

The policy data comes from Table 1 in @walker2023anticipatory, which we (or AI) turned into a spreadsheet and imported as `df.policy` – one row per *state*. That's the catch. The policy is a property of a state, and `df.adm` doesn't know what state a school is in. That information is in `df.hd`. So before we can attach the policy, we have to combine the two IPEDS dataframes.

### Combine the IPEDS Dataframes

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Coding Learning Objectives"}
- `left_join()` and `join_by()`
- `as.numeric()` and variable types
:::

`df.adm` has the applications and `df.hd` has the state. In both, a row is a *school-year* – one school in one year. UNITID identifies the school, `year` identifies the year, and together they identify the row. Variables that identify rows are called *keys*. Combining dataframes side by side – adding columns rather than stacking rows like `bind_rows()` did – is called a *join*, and it's done by matching on keys.

`df.hd` is very wide – dozens of columns of directory information – and right now we only need the state. We'll bring all of it along anyway. Columns are cheap to carry, and some of them (`CONTROL` is public/private, `INSTCAT` is the degree-granting category) may turn out to be useful for heterogeneity later. Deciding what to drop is cleaning, not combining.

Now the join. There are several kinds (more on that shortly), but the workhorse is `left_join()`. It keeps *every* row of the dataframe on the left and adds columns from the dataframe on the right that match a row on the left. Since the applications define our sample, `df.adm` goes on the left. The keys go in `join_by()`.

Here's a first try that makes the most common mistake – only using one key.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID)) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning in left_join(df.adm, df.hd, join_by(UNITID)): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 49499
```


:::
:::




Two things happened. R warned about a "many-to-many relationship," and we ended up with 49499 rows when `df.adm` only has 10011. Each school-year in `df.adm` matched *every* year for that school in `df.hd`, so every row got copied five times. If the warning doesn't make sense, paste it into AI and ask.

Look at just one school to see it happen. Alabama A&M (UNITID 100654) has one row per year in each dataframe – five rows, five years.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.adm |> filter(UNITID == 100654) |> select(UNITID, year, APPLCN)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  UNITID year  APPLCN
   <dbl> <chr>  <dbl>
1 100654 2018    9638
2 100654 2019    9579
3 100654 2020    9855
4 100654 2021    6560
5 100654 2022    8907
```


:::
:::


Join on `UNITID` alone and that one school balloons to 25 rows – every one of its five years in `df.adm` matched against every one of its five years in `df.hd`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.adm |> filter(UNITID == 100654) |>
  left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID)) |>
  select(UNITID, year.x, year.y, INSTNM)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 25 × 4
   UNITID year.x year.y INSTNM                  
    <dbl> <chr>  <chr>  <chr>                   
 1 100654 2018   2018   Alabama A & M University
 2 100654 2018   2019   Alabama A & M University
 3 100654 2018   2020   Alabama A & M University
 4 100654 2018   2021   Alabama A & M University
 5 100654 2018   2022   Alabama A & M University
 6 100654 2019   2018   Alabama A & M University
 7 100654 2019   2019   Alabama A & M University
 8 100654 2019   2020   Alabama A & M University
 9 100654 2019   2021   Alabama A & M University
10 100654 2019   2022   Alabama A & M University
# ℹ 15 more rows
```


:::
:::


Note the two `year` columns – `year.x` from `df.adm`, `year.y` from `df.hd` – dplyr's way of telling you *this column existed on both sides and I didn't know which one you meant*, which is itself a sign something is off. Every `year.x` is now paired with every possible `year.y`, which is exactly the bug. Note that R only *warned* – it didn't stop – so if you weren't paying attention, you'd carry on with a dataframe five times too big. Adding `year` to the key fixes it. Generally, the *`.x`* and `.y` suffixes indicate a *join* did not go as intended.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year)) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 10011
```


:::
:::


Add this to the workflow.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))
```
:::


One more thing before we move on. Have a look at `year`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
class(df$year)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "character"
```


:::
:::


It's a *character* – text. That's because `str_extract()` pulls text out of text, so we got `"2018"` and not `2018`. Comparisons will often still work (R quietly converts the number to text to compare them), which is exactly what makes this bug sneaky. It hides until you try to do math.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df$year[1] + 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `df$year[1] + 1`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator
```


:::
:::


Convert it with `as.numeric()` inside `mutate()`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: Know Your Types"}
Every variable has a type. The ones you'll see most are *numeric* (numbers), *character* (text), and *logical* (`TRUE`/`FALSE`). Check with `class()`.

Numbers stored as text are the most common silent bug in imported data. Check the types of your key variables before you use them.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))

#year was extracted from the file name as text; make it a number
df <- df |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year))
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
class(df$year)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "numeric"
```


:::
:::


### The Policy Indicator

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Coding Learning Objectives"}
- renaming inside `select()`: `select(new = old)`
- `if_else()`
- `right_join()`
- `join_by(x == y)` for keys with different names
- `count()`
:::

With the state attached to every school-year, we can bring in the policy. Have a look at `df.policy`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names(df.policy)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "State"                                   
[2] "Abbreviation"                            
[3] "Abortion Status"                         
[4] "Group"                                   
[5] "In Sample"                               
[6] "Note (gestational limit, if partial ban)"
```


:::
:::


Most *tidyverse* functions can handle a column name without quotations. That is `select(UNITID)` knows you are referring to a column name. However, this doesn't work if the names are numbers or have spaces. Then, you'll have to wrap the name in backticks – `` `Abortion Status` or `2021` ``– when you reference it. In @sec-walker-data-importing, we introduced `select()`. Now we'll use it again with an additional functionality. Not only does `select()` keep the specified column in the specified order, you can rename them with `new = old,` as well!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.policy |> select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`)
```
:::


After that, we can construct our policy indicator. The "Banned" states are the treatment group and everything else – including the states where a ban was blocked in court – is control. So, $Repeal_j$ from the paper is an indicator (or dummy) variable that is 1 for states that would be affected by the repeal of Roe v. Wade -- status is "Banned" in our data -- and a 0 otherwise. We need to make this variable from existing variables, `mutate()` it, so that **if** the *Abbreviation* has "Banned" in *status* it gets a 1 and **else** it gets a 0.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: Indicators and `if_else()`"}
You can mutate an **indicator** variable with `if_else().`

`if_else(condition, value if TRUE, value if FALSE)` takes three arguments – a condition, a value for `TRUE`, and a value for `FALSE` – and returns one of the two values, row by row.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if_else(status == "Banned", 1, 0)
```
:::

:::

Combining the `select()` with the `mutate()` we have


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.policy |> 
  select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0))
```
:::


Notice that we make changes to `df.policy` without assigning the changes/saving them. This means the `df.policy` dataframe in the *Environment* is the same as when it was created. This is nice because it allows us to add the variable *repeal* to `df` without changing `df.policy`. Let's try to keep it this way.

There are two ways we could perform the `join` that will bring in *repeal* to `df`. Using the `left_join()` entails operating on `df.policy` within the `join` like this


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- df |> left_join(
  df.policy |> 
    select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
    mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0))
)
```
:::


This takes only the rows on the left -- those in `df` -- and joins them to the rows on the right, a dataframe of states and repeal status.

On the other hand, we could operate on `df.policy` first and then `join` it to `df`. We want the same outcome as the `left_join()` but we want to keep only the rows that are now on the right. This is done with a `right_join()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <-  df.policy |> 
  select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |> 
  right_join(df)
```
:::


The resulting dataframes should contain the same columns (though they'll have different orders since joins try to preserve the order of the dataframe on the left) and the same rows. I will use the `right_join()` since it seems more readable to me.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: Which Join?"}
- `left_join(x, y)` keeps every row of `x`. Rows of `x` with no match get `NA`.
- `right_join(x, y)` keeps every row of `y`. Same idea, dataframes swapped.
- `inner_join(x, y)` keeps only the rows with a match in both.
- `full_join(x, y)` keeps everything.

![Which rows survive each join type, matching `df.adm` and `df.hd` on UNITID and year](images/join-types.png)

Default to `left_join()` from the dataframe that defines your sample. `right_join()` gives the same result with the arguments flipped – handy when the dataframe you're *adding* is the one coming down the pipe, as `df.policy` is here. `inner_join()` and `full_join()` change which rows survive, so use them on purpose and say so in a comment.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))

#year was extracted from the file name as text; make it a number
df <- df |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

#==== POLICY VARIABLE ====
#generate repeal indicator and join it
df <-  df.policy |> 
  select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |> 
  right_join(df)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `right_join()`:
! `by` must be supplied when `x` and `y` have no common variables.
ℹ Use `cross_join()` to perform a cross-join.
```


:::
:::


This one doesn't even produce a wrong answer – it refuses to run at all. Every dplyr join needs to know which column(s) to match on. When you don't supply `join_by()`, dplyr falls back to a *natural join*: it looks for columns with the exact same name on both sides and uses those. `df.policy` (after our `select()`) has `Abbreviation`; `df` has `STABBR`. Two different names for the same idea, so there's nothing for dplyr to find, and – **unlike** the many-to-many *warning* from earlier – this is treated as serious enough to stop the script outright rather than guess.

`join_by()` doesn't require the columns to share a name. Tell it explicitly which column on the left matches which column on the right with `==`, and it doesn't matter that they're spelled differently.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(Abbreviation == STABBR))
```
:::


Alternatively, you can use the renaming feature of `select()` to ensure both variables are named the same.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(STABBR = Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(STABBR))
```
:::


Add this to the workflow. Make sure to check your rows!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))

#year was extracted from the file name as text; make it a number
df <- df |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

#==== POLICY VARIABLE ====
#generate repeal indicator and join it
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(STABBR = Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(STABBR))
```
:::




Check the result with `count()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df |> count(repeal)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  repeal     n
   <dbl> <int>
1      0  6663
2      1  3108
3     NA   240
```


:::
:::


There are 240 school-years with no policy. Those are the not-really-states from the last chapter.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df |> filter(is.na(repeal)) |> distinct(STABBR) |> pull(STABBR)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "PR" "FM" "VI" "GU"
```


:::
:::


They'll drop out on their own in the next chapter, when we restrict to ranked schools. If they didn't, we'd have to decide what to do with them.

## Outcome Variable

The outcome in @walker2023anticipatory is the women's share of applicants. We have the number of women applicants (APPLCNW) and the number of men applicants (APPLCNM), so the share is

$$wshare = \frac{APPLCNW}{APPLCNW + APPLCNM}$$

Why not divide by the total number of applicants, APPLCN? Because IPEDS allows schools to report applicants of another or unknown gender, so APPLCN can be larger than women plus men. Women over women-plus-men is the cleaner match to the paper. This is a `mutate()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df |> mutate(wshare = APPLCNW/(APPLCNW + APPLCNM)) |> select(wshare) |> datasummary_skim()
```

A share should live between 0 and 1, and it does. The mean is a bit above one half, which is what we expect – women have been the majority of college applicants for a while. Some school-years are missing because a school reported zero (or nothing) for both, which makes the share undefined. We'll deal with those in the next chapter, when we clean the data.

Let's add the outcome variable to our workflow.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))

#year was extracted from the file name as text; make it a number
df <- df |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

#==== POLICY VARIABLE ====
#generate repeal indicator and join it
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(STABBR = Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(STABBR))

#==== OUTCOME VARIABLE ====
df <- df |> mutate(wshare = APPLCNW/(APPLCNW + APPLCNM) )
```
:::




## Heterogeneous Variables

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Coding Learning Objectives"}
- long vs. wide formats
- `pivot_longer()`
- `distinct()`
:::

Policies will have different impacts across groups. This is often called heterogeneous impacts. For example, this ban might affect community colleges differently than public universities. In fact, @walker2023anticipatory operationalize this with a single variable, the U.S. News & World Report Rankings. But, other variables, like the amount of online students or whether a school is public or private might also show heterogeneous impacts. It's generally good to keep the outcome, policy, and heterogeneous variables in places where you can readily find them. You might later want to look at a different outcome, slightly different policy, or heterogeneous effects. Actually, @walker2023anticipatory does all of these. They examine the impact of bans on a different outcome – total applications (Figure A5), policy (dropping states that blocked bans) \[Figure A7\], and heterogeneity by ranking \[Figures A1 and A3\] and out-of-state applications \[Figures A2 and A4\]. All of these investigations are central to understanding *how* the policy affects applications.

We have the ranking dataframe, which we will join shortly.

However, the IPEDS EF-C survey tells the number of freshmen by home state at a school. You should use this data to generate a variable representing out-of-state freshmen enrollment as a proxy for applications[^walker-make-variables-1] and replicate the heterogeneity analysis noted above in @walker2023anticipatory.

[^walker-make-variables-1]: It is hard to tell from the paper, but there is a chance @walker2023anticipatory did this, too.

The two dataframes give different numbers of rows! That's because `df.rank` has one row per subject (school) and each measurement (year-rank) has its own column. The unit of observation is a school. This is called a wide format.

`df` has a row for each subject-measurement (school-year) with all the measurements in one column – *wshare* (for example). The unit of observation is a school-year. This is called a long format.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: Long vs. Wide"}
**Wide**: one row per subject, one column per measurement. `df.rank` is wide – one row per school, one column per year.

**Long**: one row per subject-measurement, with the measurement identifier stored as a variable. `df` is long – one row per school-year, with `year` as a column.
:::

Importantly, most computational regression functions want long format dataframes.

To put `df.rank` into a long format, we use another *tidyverse* function, `pivot_longer()`. We tell it to take the year columns (currently named 2026, 2025, etc.) and place the names into a single variable called *year*. Also, the values in those columns -- which are the ranks in that year -- should go into a column called *rank*.

![`pivot_longer()` stacks each year's column into a `year` column and a `rank` column, turning one row per school into one row per school-year](images/pivot-long-wide.png)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df.rank.long <- df.rank |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = `2026`:`1984`,  
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "rank")
```
:::


From here, we could join this with `df`, preserving the rows in `df`, provided we make the *year* variable in `df.rank.long` numeric first (the same text-vs-number problem from earlier – column names are always text).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- df |>
  left_join(
    #format df.rank.long to have numerical year and UNITID cols
    df.rank.long |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year),UNITID = IPEDS),
    join_by(UNITID,year)
  )
```
:::


But, since all we want is the 2023 rank, it is overkill.

So, instead, we can select the IPEDS and *2023* columns from `df.rank` (renaming them on the way) and join that to `df`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- df.rank |> select(UNITID = IPEDS,rank2023 = `2023`) |> 
  right_join(df,join_by(UNITID))
```
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
#MAKE VARIABLES
#assumes import data.R has been run: df.rank, df.adm, df.hd, df.policy

#==== COMBINE IPEDS DATA ====
#add directory information to the applications data
df <- df.adm |> left_join(df.hd, join_by(UNITID, year))

#year was extracted from the file name as text; make it a number
df <- df |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

#==== POLICY VARIABLE ====
#generate repeal indicator and join it
df <-  df.policy |>
  select(STABBR = Abbreviation, status = `Abortion Status`) |>
  mutate(repeal = if_else(status == "Banned",1,0)) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(STABBR))

#==== OUTCOME VARIABLE ====
df <- df |> mutate(wshare = APPLCNW/(APPLCNW + APPLCNM) )

#==== HETEROGENEOUS VARIABLES ====
#select 2023 rank and join
df <- df.rank |> select(UNITID=IPEDS,rank2023 = `2023`) |>
  right_join(df,join_by(UNITID))
```

## Save the Script

The final step is to give the script a name – *make variables.R* – and save it in `scripts/data processing`.

## What's Next

`df` now has one row per school-year with the policy (*repeal*), the outcome (*wshare*), and the heterogeneity variable (*rank2023*) – everything the analysis needs. What it doesn't have yet is the paper's *sample*. It still has every school IPEDS knows about, including the unranked ones, the not-really-states, and the school-years with an undefined share. Restricting to the paper's sample is cleaning, and that's the next chapter.
